output.answer:
`weave.init()` initializes your project so Weave can trace your Python code. Pass your project as `"[YOUR-TEAM]/[YOUR-PROJECT]"`.

**What it does**
- It registers your team and project with Weave, so the SDK routes spans to the correct location in the UI [S2].
- In the agent quickstart, it authenticates with Weights & Biases and configures the OTel exporter that sends agent spans to the Agents view [S1].
- The argument is a project name that Weave uses to organize your traces [S3].
- For agent tracing, call it before `start_conversation()`, `start_turn()` and the other start calls. Those functions no-op silently when the init call is absent [S2].

**What to pass**
- Replace `[YOUR-TEAM]` with your CoreWeave Forge team name and `[YOUR-PROJECT]` with your Weights & Biases project name [S2].
- If the project doesn't exist on your team, Weave creates it the first time you write to it [S1].
- Some integration examples pass only a project name, such as `weave.init("langchain_demo")` [S3]. The pages I read don't explain how a bare name is resolved. The team/project form is the one the agent docs show.

```python
import weave

# Placeholders: use your own team and project names
weave.init("my-team/my-project")
```

sources.heading: Before you begin
sources.page_context:
# Trace your agents

> Use the Weave SDK to instrument multi-turn agentic applications and view them in the Agents tab.

> [!TIP]
>
> **This workflow is also available in CoreWeave Agent Lens.** Agent Lens is the Forge experience built for tracing, monitoring, and analyzing AI agents, with automated insights into agent failures and user intents. It uses the same trace data as Weights & Biases Weave, so the traces you already send appear there with nothing to migrate.
> [See how to do this in Agent Lens](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/agent-lens/tracing/instrument.md).

Learn how to instrument a multi-turn agentic application using the W\&B Weave SDK so that you can view, debug, and evaluate your agent's behavior. This guide is intended for developers who build or integrate agents and want structured visibility into conversations, turns, LLM calls, and tool executions.

The Weave SDK for Agents models the full lifecycle of a multi-turn agent conversation: the agent that owns many conversations, the conversation that groups turns together, each user-agent exchange (turn), the LLM calls within a turn, and the tool executions that an LLM triggers. Traces appear in the **Agents** tab of your Weave project. Each conversation shows a multi-turn timeline with nested tool calls, token usage, and feedback.

Weave is built on [OpenTelemetry (OTel)](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/), the open standard for distributed tracing. Every turn, LLM call, and tool call emits an OTel *span* (a structured record of one operation). Each span is tagged with [GenAI semantic-convention](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/) attributes like `gen_ai.agent.name` and `gen_ai.conversation.id`.

If you're tracing individual functions as Ops with the `@weave.op` decorator, see [Trace LLM applications](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/tracing.md) instead.

# Quickstart: Set up custom agent observability

> Trace a multi-turn agent with the Weave SDK. Conversations, turns, LLM calls, and tool calls render in the Agents view of your project.

> [!TIP]
>
> **This workflow is also available in CoreWeave Agent Lens.** Agent Lens is the Forge experience built for tracing, monitoring, and analyzing AI agents, with automated insights into agent failures and user intents. It uses the same trace data as Weights & Biases Weave, so the traces you already send appear there with nothing to migrate.
> [See how to do this in Agent Lens](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/agent-lens/get-started/custom-agents.md).

[Try in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/github/wandb/examples/blob/main/colabs/weave/custom-agents-quickstart.ipynb) · [GitHub source](https://github.com/wandb/examples/blob/main/colabs/weave/custom-agents-quickstart.ipynb)

The Weave SDK lets you trace agents built with popular SDKs or custom harnesses. This quickstart shows you how to manually integrate Weave into a custom-built multi-turn agent to emit and capture OpenTelemetry spans. For conceptual understanding about Weave for agents, see [Trace your agents](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/trace-agents.md).

If you're looking to integrate Weave with SDKs or harnesses such as the Claude Agent SDK or Codex, see [Choose an agent integration](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/agent-integration-quickstart.md). Weave autopatches into several agent-building SDKs and agent harnesses for quick integration.

sources.heading: Getting started
sources.text:
## Getting started

To get started, call `weave.init()` at the beginning of your script. The argument to `weave.init()` is a project name that Weave uses to organize your traces.

```python lines {6} theme={"system"}
import weave
from langchain_core.prompts import PromptTemplate
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI

# Initialize Weave with your project name
weave.init("langchain_demo")

llm = ChatOpenAI()
prompt = PromptTemplate.from_template("1 + {number} = ")

llm_chain = prompt | llm

output = llm_chain.invoke({"number": 2})

print(output)
```

# LangChain

> Use Weave to track and log all calls made through the LangChain Python library

[Try in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/github/wandb/examples/blob/master/weave/docs/quickstart_langchain.ipynb)

Weave tracks and logs calls made through the [LangChain Python library](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langchain).

When working with LLMs, debugging is part of the job. Whether a model call fails, an output is misformatted, or nested model calls create confusion, pinpointing issues can be hard. LangChain applications often consist of multiple steps and LLM call invocations, so it helps to understand the inner workings of your chains and agents.

Weave captures traces for your [LangChain](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langchain/overview) applications automatically. This lets you monitor and analyze your application's performance, which makes it easier to debug and optimize your LLM workflows.

This guide is for developers building LangChain applications who want to add tracing, evaluation, and observability with Weave. It walks through enabling automatic tracing, attaching metadata, controlling tracing manually, and wrapping LangChain chains as Weave models for evaluation.

results.heading: Publish an object
results.snippet:
## Publish an object

Weave's serialization layer saves and versions objects.

**Python**

```python lines theme={"system"}
import weave
weave.init("your-team-name/your-project-name")
# Save a list, giving it the name 'cat-names'
weave.publish(['felix', 'jimbo', 'billie'], 'cat-names')
```

**TypeScript**

TypeScript publishing support is limited. Not all objects are supported.

```typescript twoslash lines theme={"system"}
// @noErrors
import * as weave from 'weave'

const client = await weave.init("your-team-name/your-project-name")

// Save an array, giving it the name 'cat-names'
client.publish(['felix', 'jimbo', 'billie'], 'cat-names')
```

When you save an object with a name, Weave creates the first version of that object if it doesn't exist.

# Trace your agents

> Use the Weave SDK to instrument multi-turn agentic applications and view them in the Agents tab.

> [!TIP]
>
> **This workflow is also available in CoreWeave Agent Lens.** Agent Lens is the Forge experience built for tracing, monitoring, and analyzing AI agents, with automated insights into agent failures and user intents. It uses the same trace data as Weights & Biases Weave, so the traces you already send appear there with nothing to migrate.
> [See how to do this in Agent Lens](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/agent-lens/tracing/instrument.md).

Learn how to instrument a multi-turn agentic application using the W\&B Weave SDK so that you can view, debug, and evaluate your agent's behavior. This guide is intended for developers who build or integrate agents and want structured visibility into conversations, turns, LLM calls, and tool executions.

The Weave SDK for Agents models the full lifecycle of a multi-turn agent conversation: the agent that owns many conversations, the conversation that groups turns together, each user-agent exchange (turn), the LLM calls within a turn, and the tool executions that an LLM triggers. Traces appear in the **Agents** tab of your Weave project. Each conversation shows a multi-turn timeline with nested tool calls, token usage, and feedback.

Weave is built on [OpenTelemetry (OTel)](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/), the open standard for distributed tracing. Every turn, LLM call, and tool call emits an OTel *span* (a structured record of one operation). Each span is tagged with [GenAI semantic-convention](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/) attributes like `gen_ai.agent.name` and `gen_ai.conversation.id`.

If you're tracing individual functions as Ops with the `@weave.op` decorator, see [Trace LLM applications](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/tracing.md) instead.

## Getting started

To get started, call `weave.init()` at the beginning of your script. The argument to `weave.init()` is a project name that Weave uses to organize your traces.

```python lines {6} theme={"system"}
import weave
from langchain_core.prompts import PromptTemplate
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI

# Initialize Weave with your project name
weave.init("langchain_demo")

llm = ChatOpenAI()
prompt = PromptTemplate.from_template("1 + {number} = ")

llm_chain = prompt | llm

output = llm_chain.invoke({"number": 2})

print(output)
```

Weave tracks and logs calls made through the [LangChain Python library](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langchain).

When working with LLMs, debugging is part of the job. Whether a model call fails, an output is misformatted, or nested model calls create confusion, pinpointing issues can be hard. LangChain applications often consist of multiple steps and LLM call invocations, so it helps to understand the inner workings of your chains and agents.

Weave captures traces for your [LangChain](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langchain/overview) applications automatically. This lets you monitor and analyze your application's performance, which makes it easier to debug and optimize your LLM workflows.

This guide is for developers building LangChain applications who want to add tracing, evaluation, and observability with Weave. It walks through enabling automatic tracing, attaching metadata, controlling tracing manually, and wrapping LangChain chains as Weave models for evaluation.

`weave.init()` sets up Weave tracing for your Python script. The string you pass is your project, normally written as `"<team>/<project>"`.

**What it does**
- It initializes your project. The docs say this registers your team and project with Weave so the SDK routes spans to the correct place in the UI [S2].
- In the agent quickstart, it authenticates with Weights & Biases and configures the OTel exporter that sends agent spans to the Agents view [S1].
- The argument is a project name that Weave uses to organize your traces [S3].
- Call it before agent tracing calls such as `start_conversation()` or `start_turn()`. Those functions silently do nothing if the init call is absent [S2]. Put it at the start of your script [S3].

**What to pass**
- Use `"[YOUR-TEAM]/[YOUR-PROJECT]"`. That means your CoreWeave Forge team name, then your Weights & Biases project name [S2].
- If the project doesn't exist on your team, Weave creates it the first time you write to it [S1].
- Some integration examples pass only a bare name, such as `weave.init("langchain_demo")` [S3]. I didn't find a statement in the pages I read about how a bare name resolves to a team. The team/project form is the one the agent docs show.

```python
import weave

# Replace the placeholders with your own team and project names
weave.init("my-team/my-project")
```

Your `WANDB_API_KEY` must be available too. The quickstart sets it as an environment variable [S1].
